newsitem.title: JAMAICA: Int'l seabed authority to review mining code.
newsitem.headline: Int'l seabed authority to review mining code.

text.p: The International Seabed Authority (ISA) began its third session Monday afternoon with the aim of beginning work on a new deep seabed mining code that would regulate the activities of governments and companies that wish to begin mining the ocean floor.

Delegates from the 133 ISA member countries have been given a set of 41 draft regulations that will be considered at this session, set to end March 27 and resume again in August, at which time final approval is expected.

The draft mining code is the first substantive matter to be taken up by the ISA since its inauguration two years ago. Deep seabed mining was one of the main reasons for the creation of the United Nations Law of the Sea Treaty, which came into force in 1994 and established the ISA.

The draft regulations cover prospecting and exploration for polymetallic nodules that lie on or just beneath the ocean floor. So far exploration has focused on three zones in the Pacific and Indian oceans, by seven pioneer investors approved between 1987 and 1994.

The seven -- the Indian government, IFREMER (France), DORD (Japan), Yuzhmorgeologiya (Russia), COMRA (China), Interoceanmetal Joint Organization (Bulgaria, Cuba, Czech and Slovak republics, Poland and Russia), and the South Korean government -- will have their present arrangements reviewed.
Under the new regulations, prospecting is open to all, requiring only that the ISA be notified. Exploration cannot begin until a work plan is submitted, and each investor is given a 15-year license.

Every area also assigned must be large enough and contain sufficient resources to allow two mining operations, one to be reserved for the ISA or developing countries. The ISA will establish its own mining arm, but will initially be restricted to joint ventures with governments or private firms.
The polymetallic nodules contain manganese, nickel, cobalt and copper. Commercial exploitation is not expected for at least another decade.

In addition to working on the new mining code, the ISA will select a 15-member finance committee, and finalize agreements covering its relations with the United Nations and the Jamaican government. The ISA is headquartered in Kingston.
